en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek has no verb here.

01.r: The Spirit of God, resting on the speaker.
01.n: Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint uses it chiefly for Hebrew רוּחַ, and that its first senses are wind and breath.

02.n: There is no article in the Greek. Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint uses this word chiefly for יהוה, God's name.

04.r: The speaker, Jesus, reading the passage.
04.n: The full, accented form of the pronoun, which can give it weight: 'upon me'.

05.r: With the next word, forms the phrase 'on account of which'.

06.r: Gives the ground of the Spirit's presence: the anointing.
06.n: Literally 'on account of which'; Abbott-Smith gives the word as 'on account of, because of', and notes this verse's old Ionic spelling, εἵνεκεν. The DRC's 'Wherefore' reads it as 'for which reason'.

07.r: God has set him apart for his task, as by anointing with oil.
07.n: Abbott-Smith says the Septuagint uses it chiefly for Hebrew מָשַׁח, of consecration to a sacred office: priest, prophet, king. In the New Testament it is metaphorical, of God's anointing. An aorist: 'he anointed'.

09.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to bring or announce glad tidings', and notes the Septuagint's use of it for Hebrew בָּשַׂר. English 'evangelise' comes from it; 'preach the gospel' is the KJV's rendering.
t: that I should preach the Gospel

10.r: Those with nothing, who must depend on others.
10.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from πτώσσω, to crouch, cower: one who crouches and cowers. As a noun he gives 'a beggar'. The Septuagint uses it for Hebrew עָנִי and דַּל.

11.r: God has sent him on a mission.
11.n: A perfect tense: the sending stands, and he is now on that mission. Abbott-Smith: 'to send away, to dispatch on service', and 'to send with a commission'.

18.r: To announce publicly, as a herald does.
18.n: Abbott-Smith: 'to be a herald, to proclaim', citing this verse and the next.

19.r: Those taken captive, as in war.
19.n: Abbott-Smith builds it from αἰχμή, a spear, and ἁλίσκομαι, to be taken: one taken by the spear. The Septuagint uses it chiefly for Hebrew שָׁבָה; this verse, a quotation of the Septuagint, is its only New Testament occurrence.

20.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense, 'dismissal, release', is the one he gives for this verse; the second is the forgiveness of sins. He notes that the Septuagint uses the word for Hebrew יוֹבֵל, jubilee, and דְּרוֹר, liberty. This study renders it 'release' in both its places in the verse.

23.r: Sight given back to the blind.
23.n: Built on the verb 'to look up' or 'to see again'. Abbott-Smith gives 'recovery of sight', its only Septuagint use being Isa. 61:1 and its only New Testament use this verse.

24.r: To send the broken away free.
24.n: The same verb as 'he has sent' earlier in the verse. With 'in release' it means to send them off as free people; most translations fold the phrase into 'set at liberty' or 'release'.
t: that I should set at libertie

25.r: People broken down by what has been done to them.
25.n: A perfect passive participle: those who have been broken and remain so. Abbott-Smith gives 'to break in pieces, shatter', and metaphorically 'to break down'; this verse, a Septuagint quotation, is its only New Testament occurrence.

26.r: The state in which they are sent away.

27.r: The second 'release' of the verse: freedom for the broken.
27.n: The same noun as 'release to captives' above. The repetition is hidden in translations that render the phrase 'set at liberty'.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus adds ἰάσασθαι τοὺς συντετριμμένους τὴν καρδίαν, 'to heal those broken in heart', after 'he has sent me'. That is the KJV's 'to heal the brokenhearted'; our text, like the ASV and BSB, lacks it. It also reads the present infinitive εὐαγγελίζεσθαι for the aorist, with no difference in English.
